tool.name: Beautiful Soup
tool.tagline: Parse, search and edit HTML and XML in Python, even when it's badly broken
tool.description: Beautiful Soup (the bs4 package) parses HTML and XML into a tree of Python objects that you can search with find_all or CSS selectors, navigate and modify. It's the most popular tool for web scraping and for cleaning or transforming HTML, and it copes gracefully with the malformed markup found on real websites.

glossary.def: A Python library that reads HTML (or XML) text and turns it into a tree of Python objects you can search, so you can pull data out of web pages.

A marker in angle brackets, like

or

, that starts or ends a piece of a web page. In Beautiful Soup, a Tag object is one such element in the parsed tree.
In HTML, a label in an element's class attribute (class="price") that groups similar elements, mainly for styling. In Python, a class is a blueprint for creating objects.
In HTML, an attribute that gives one element a name unique on the page, like id="main".
An HTML attribute whose name starts with data-, like data-id="42", that sites add to store their own information on an element.
The programming language that runs inside web browsers; pages use it to load data and change what you see after the page arrives.
Nickname for the BeautifulSoup object: the whole parsed document, and the starting point for every search.
A code HTML uses to write a character that would otherwise be confusing or hard to type, like & for & or é for é.
A short pattern from CSS that picks elements on a page, like div.price (div elements with class price) or #main (the element with id main).
Tools built into every desktop browser (right-click, Inspect) that show a page's elements, the requests it makes, and more.
A piece of text in the parsed tree, sitting between or inside tags; even the line breaks and spaces between tags become text nodes.
In a tree, a node with the same parent as another one, like two <li> items in the same list.
A file at the root of a website (example.com/robots.txt) that tells automated programs which parts they may and may not fetch.
Garbled text such as CafÃ© instead of Café, caused by reading bytes with the wrong text encoding.
Structured data some pages embed in a <script type="application/ld+json"> tag, describing things like a product's name and price as JSON.
A set of <meta property="og:..."> tags pages use to describe themselves (title, image) for link previews on social media.
A real web browser controlled by a program, with no window on screen; it runs a page's JavaScript so the program can read the finished page.
A Beautiful Soup filter you give while parsing, so only matching tags are built into the tree and the rest is skipped.
Beautiful Soup's type for a piece of text in the tree: a normal Python string that also knows its place, like its parent tag.
In Beautiful Soup, the setting that decides how special characters are written when the tree is turned back into HTML text.

An HTML element that never has content or a closing tag, such as
or .
A fast add-on Python library for reading HTML and XML, written in C; Beautiful Soup can use it as its parser.
A Python library that reads HTML exactly the way web browsers do; accurate but slow. Beautiful Soup can use it as its parser.

concepts.name: What a web page is made of: HTML
concepts.summary: Read the HTML behind a web page: tags, elements, attributes like class and id, and how elements nest into a tree.
concepts.why: Beautiful Soup works on HTML, so you need to be able to read it before you can pull data out of it.
concepts.body:
Every web page you visit is, underneath, a text file. Your **browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) downloads that text and draws the page from it. The text is written in **HTML**, a format that marks up content with labels saying what each piece is: a heading, a paragraph, a link, a list. The labels are **tags**: words in angle brackets. `

` opens a paragraph and `

`, with a slash, closes it. A pair of tags plus everything between them is an **element**: ```html

Rain expected tomorrow

``` Elements sit inside other elements. A list `
    ` contains list items `
  • `, and the whole page sits inside ``, split into a `` (information about the page, such as its ``) and a `<body>` (what you see). Because of this nesting, a page forms a **tree**, like a family tree: each element has one parent and can have children. Elements with the same parent are siblings. An opening tag can carry **attributes**: extra name="value" settings. A link is `<a href="/news">News</a>`; its `href` attribute holds the address the link goes to. Three attributes matter a lot for finding data: - `class` puts a label on elements so they can be styled alike. Every price on a shop page might have `class="price"`. An element can have several classes, separated by spaces. - `id` gives one element a name that is unique on the page, like `id="main"`. - `data-` attributes, like `data-id="42"`, hold extra information a site stores for its own use. Many pages also include programs written in **JavaScript**, a programming language browsers run. They can change the page after it has arrived; keep that in mind, because Beautiful Soup only sees the HTML text itself. To see the HTML of any page, right-click it and choose "View page source".
concepts.code:
Headlines

  • Markets rally
  • Rain expected
Older stories
takeaways:
A web page is HTML text: tags like

and

mark elements
Elements nest inside each other, forming a tree of parents and children
Attributes such as href, class, id and data-* sit in the opening tag
class labels groups of elements; id names one element
pitfalls: Assuming everything you see in the browser is in the page's HTML; JavaScript may have added it later.

quiz.q:
In
  • Rain expected
    • , what is class="story"?
options: An attribute that labels the element
quiz.explain: Name="value" settings inside the opening tag are attributes; class is the one used to label groups of elements.

quiz.q: A <ul> contains two <li> elements. How are the two <li> elements related?
options: They are siblings: both children of the ul
The first is the parent of the second
They are attributes of the ul
quiz.explain: Elements that share a parent are siblings in the tree.

concepts.name: Parsing HTML into a soup
concepts.summary: Install Beautiful Soup, turn an HTML string into a searchable tree with an explicit parser, and look at it.
concepts.why: Every Beautiful Soup task starts by turning HTML text into a tree you can search, and naming the parser avoids surprises.
concepts.body:
To a Python program, a page's HTML is just one long string. Finding "the second price on the page" in that string by hand is painful. A program first has to read the text and work out its structure: which tags open and close where, and what sits inside what. That is called **parsing**, and the piece of code that does it is a parser.

**Beautiful Soup** parses HTML, even badly broken HTML, into a tree of Python objects you can search and move around in. It also reads XML, a similar tag-based format used for data. Pulling data out of web pages automatically like this is called **web scraping**, and Beautiful Soup is the most popular tool for it.

Install it with Python's installer, `pip install beautifulsoup4`, and import it from the `bs4` package.

Create a **soup** (the parsed document) with `BeautifulSoup(markup, "html.parser")`. The markup can be a string, bytes or an open file. The second argument chooses the parser:

- `"html.parser"`: comes with Python, nothing extra to install.
- `"lxml"`: much faster, needs `pip install lxml`.
- `"html5lib"`: reads HTML exactly the way a browser does, but is the slowest.

Always name the parser. If you leave it out, Beautiful Soup picks the best one installed and prints a warning, so the same code can give different results on different computers.

The `BeautifulSoup` object is the root of the tree. Useful first steps:

- `soup.title` gives the first `<title>` tag; `soup.title.string` its text.
- `soup.prettify()` returns the document re-indented, one tag per line, for reading.
- `print(soup)` or `str(soup)` gives the (repaired) HTML back.

Beautiful Soup doesn't download pages and doesn't run JavaScript; it only parses the text you give it. To fetch pages from the internet you pair it with a download library such as Requests (covered later).
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """ Daily News

Headlines

Markets rally

Rain expected

""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") print(soup.title) # Daily News print(soup.title.string) # Daily News print(soup.h1["id"]) # top print(soup.p) #

Markets rally

print(soup.prettify()[:40].splitlines()[:3]) # ['', ' ', ' ']
takeaways: pip install beautifulsoup4, then import from bs4
BeautifulSoup(markup, 'html.parser') builds the tree
Always name the parser explicitly
It parses only; downloading pages and running JavaScript are not its job
pitfalls: Omitting the parser argument and getting different results on another machine.

quiz.q: Why should you pass the parser name to BeautifulSoup()?
options: It is required, or it raises
Otherwise the best installed parser is chosen, so results can differ between computers
quiz.explain: Different parsers repair broken HTML differently; naming one gives the same result everywhere.

concepts.name: Tags, attributes and text
concepts.summary: Read a tag's name, attributes and text with ['attr'], .get(), .attrs, .string and get_text().
concepts.why: Extracting data means reading attributes like href and the text inside tags correctly.
concepts.body:
Each element in the tree is a **Tag** object. `soup.a` returns the first `` anywhere in the document. You can chain these: `soup.body.p` means "the first `

` inside the first ``". **Attributes** work like a dict: - `tag["href"]` returns the value, raising `KeyError` if the attribute is missing. - `tag.get("href")` returns `None` (or a default you give) instead: use it for attributes that may not be there. - `tag.attrs` is the full dict; `tag.has_attr("data-id")` checks whether one exists. - Attributes that can hold several values, most importantly `class`, come back as a **list**: `["btn", "primary"]`. **Text** has several ways in: - `tag.string`: the text, but only when the tag contains exactly one thing. It is `None` when the tag contains more, such as text plus a ``. - `tag.get_text()`: all text inside, joined together. `get_text(" ", strip=True)` joins the pieces with a space and trims spaces and line breaks around each, which is what you usually want. - `tag.stripped_strings`: the non-blank text pieces, one by one, for use in a `for` loop or `list()`. `tag.name` is the tag's name (`"a"`), and you can rename the tag by assigning to it. HTML writes some characters as codes called **entities**, such as `&` for `&`. Beautiful Soup turns them back into the real characters, so the text you get is ordinary Python text. Most bugs at this stage are about `None`: a tag that isn't there (`soup.find(...)` returning `None`), or `.string` being `None`. Check before you chain another step onto it.
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """
Desk lamp & bulb 19.99
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") card, link = soup.div, soup.a print(card["class"]) # ['card', 'featured'] print(card["data-id"], card.get("missing")) # 42 None print(link.attrs) # {'href': '/item/42', 'title': 'Lamp'} print(link.string) # None: several children print(link.get_text()) # Desk lamp & bulb print(soup.find("span").get_text(strip=True)) # 19.99 print(list(card.stripped_strings)) # ['Desk', 'lamp', '& bulb', '19.99']
takeaways: tag['x'] raises on missing attributes; tag.get('x') returns None
class is a list of classes
.string is None when a tag has several children; use get_text()
get_text(' ', strip=True) for clean text
pitfalls: Calling .string on a tag with nested markup and getting None.

quiz.explain: The p has two children (a string and a b tag), so .string can't pick one and returns None.

concepts.name: Searching with find and find_all
concepts.summary: Search the tree with find() and find_all() by tag name, attributes, class_, string and limit.
concepts.why: find and find_all do most of the work in pulling data out of pages; nearly every scraper is built from them.
concepts.body:
`find_all(...)` returns a list of all matching tags inside the current one (a `ResultSet`, which works like a list). `find()` returns the first match, or **`None`** when there isn't one.

Ways to filter:

- By name: `soup.find_all("a")`.
- By attribute, as a keyword argument: `soup.find_all(id="main")`, or `soup.find_all(href=True)` for "has an href at all".
- By class: `soup.find_all("div", class_="price")`. Matching works on any one of the tag's classes.
- Attributes whose names aren't valid Python names, such as `data-id` with its hyphen, go in a dict: `attrs={"data-id": "42"}`.
- By text: `string="Next"` matches tags whose `.string` is exactly that.
- `limit=5` stops after five matches; `recursive=False` looks only at direct children.

Why `class_` with an underscore? `class` is a **keyword** in Python: a word the language reserves for itself, so you can't use it as an argument name.

Calling a tag like a function is shorthand for `find_all`: `soup("a")` is the same as `soup.find_all("a")`.

You can call these methods on any tag, and they then search only inside that tag. That's the main way to narrow a search: first find the element that wraps the part you care about (one product card, one table), then search inside it.

Remember that `find()` returning `None` is normal for optional content. `soup.find("span").text` crashes with `AttributeError: 'NoneType'` when the span is missing.
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """
  • Kettle 25
  • Toaster 40
  • Blender
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") items = soup.find_all("li", class_="item") print(len(items)) # 3 print(soup.find("li", class_="sale").a.string) # Kettle print([a["href"] for a in soup.find_all("a", href=True)]) # ['/p/1', '/p/2'] print(soup.find(attrs={"data-id": "2"}).a.string) # Toaster print(soup.find("a", string="Blender")) # Blender for li in items: price = li.find("span", class_="price") print(li.a.string, price.string if price else "n/a") # Kettle 25 / Toaster 40 / Blender n/a
takeaways: find_all returns all matches, find the first or None
class_= for classes, attrs={...} for names like data-id
href=True means 'has this attribute'
Search inside a wrapping tag to narrow results
pitfalls: Chaining .text on find() results without handling None.

quiz.q: Which call finds <div class="price big"> by class?
quiz.explain: class_ avoids the keyword clash and matches any one of the tag's classes.

concepts.name: CSS selectors with select()
concepts.summary: Use select() and select_one() with CSS selectors for short, precise searches.
concepts.why: CSS selectors are a compact way to point at elements, and you can try them out in the browser before writing code.
concepts.body:
Websites style their pages with **CSS**, a language that says "make every price red, make the title big". To say which elements a style applies to, CSS uses short patterns called **selectors**: `.price` means "elements with class price", `#main` means "the element with id main". Beautiful Soup lets you search with the same patterns.

`soup.select("selector")` returns a list of all matching tags; `soup.select_one(...)` returns the first or `None`. They're powered by the **soupsieve** library, which is installed along with Beautiful Soup.

Selectors you'll use constantly:

- `div.price` (a div with class price), `#main`, `a[href]` (an a that has an href), `a[href^="https"]` (href starts with https), `img[src$=".png"]` (ends with .png), `[data-id="42"]`.
- Inside: `ul li` (an li anywhere inside a ul), `ul > li` (an li directly inside a ul), `h2 + p` (the p right after an h2), `h2 ~ p` (any p after an h2, same parent).
- Position and text: `li:nth-of-type(2)` (the second li), `tr:not(.header)` (rows without class header), `p:-soup-contains("Price")` (a p whose text contains Price; a soupsieve extra).
- Several at once: `h1, h2, h3`.

Like `find_all`, `select` works on any tag to search only inside it: `card.select_one(".price")`.

Which to use? `select` shines for structure (directly inside, the n-th one, starts with), and you can test a selector in your browser first. `find_all` is handier with Python values, such as text patterns or your own functions (a later lesson). Many scrapers mix both.

Every desktop browser has **developer tools** (right-click a page, then Inspect) that show the page's elements and can copy a selector for one. Be careful with copied selectors: they're often absurdly specific (`div:nth-child(3) > div > span`) and break with the next redesign. Prefer selectors built on stable classes, ids or `data-` attributes.
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """

Specs

Weight: 1.2 kg

Color: red

  • A
  • B
  • Ad
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") print(soup.select_one("#post > h2").string) # Specs print([p.string for p in soup.select("h2 ~ p")]) # ['Weight: 1.2 kg', 'Color: red'] print([a["href"] for a in soup.select('ul.links li:not(.ad) a[href^="https"]')]) # ['https://x.io/a'] print(soup.select_one('p:-soup-contains("Color")').string) # Color: red print(soup.select_one(".missing")) # None
takeaways: select() returns a list, select_one() the first match or None
Attribute operators ^= $= *= and combinators > + ~ are supported
:-soup-contains() matches by text
Prefer stable classes, ids and data attributes over positional selectors
pitfalls: Pasting long nth-child selectors from the developer tools that break on the next layout change.

options: Every li anywhere in the document
li elements that are direct children of a ul
The first li of each ul
quiz.explain: > is the child combinator, so only li tags directly inside a ul match.

concepts.name: Navigating the tree
concepts.summary: Move around the tree with parent, children, descendants, siblings and the find_parent/find_next_sibling family.
concepts.why: Data often lives next to a label or inside an ancestor, and navigation methods let you reach it relative to something you can find.
concepts.body: Every tag and every piece of text in the tree is a **node**. Once you have one, you can move from it: - **Down**: `.contents` (a list of direct children), `.children` (the same, for looping), `.descendants` (every node below, at any depth, including text). - **Up**: `.parent`, `.parents` (each ancestor in turn, up to the soup). - **Sideways**: `.next_sibling`, `.previous_sibling`, `.next_siblings`. - **Document order**: `.next_element` / `.previous_element` walk through the nodes in the order they appear in the HTML, crossing tag boundaries. The classic gotcha: the spaces and line breaks between tags are kept in the tree as **text nodes**. In `a\nb`, the first td's `.next_sibling` is the string `"\n"`, not the next td. That's why the methods that **search while they move** are usually better: - `find_next_sibling("td")`, `find_next_siblings(...)`, `find_previous_sibling(...)`. - `find_parent("table")`, `find_parents(...)`. - `find_next("a")`, `find_all_next(...)`: anything later in the document. They accept the same filters as `find`, so `label.find_next_sibling("span", class_="value")` skips whitespace and unrelated tags. A common scraping pattern: locate a stable **label** by its text (`soup.find("th", string="Price")`) and move from it to the value next to it, rather than relying on positions that change.
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """
BrandAcme
Price49 EUR
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") th = soup.find("th", string="Price") print(th.find_next_sibling("td").string) # 49 EUR print(th.parent.name, th.find_parent("table")["id"]) # tr specs first_row = soup.find("tr") print(repr(first_row.next_sibling)) # '\n': whitespace text node print(first_row.find_next_sibling("tr").th.string) # Price print([c.name for c in first_row.children]) # ['th', 'td'] print([type(n).__name__ for n in soup.table.descendants][:4]) # ['NavigableString', 'Tag', 'Tag', 'NavigableString']
takeaways: .children/.descendants go down, .parent/.parents up, siblings sideways
Whitespace between tags is a text node in .next_sibling
find_next_sibling / find_parent filter while navigating
Find a stable label, then navigate to its value
pitfalls: Using .next_sibling and getting '\n' instead of the next tag.

quiz.q: Why can tr.next_sibling be '\n' instead of the next <tr>?
options: The whitespace between tags is kept as a text node in the tree
quiz.explain: Newlines and indentation between tags are NavigableStrings and count as siblings.

concepts.name: Advanced filters: regex, lists and functions
concepts.summary: Pass regular expressions, lists, True and your own functions to find_all for flexible matching.
concepts.why: Real pages need looser matching (any heading, links to PDFs, tags that have some attribute) that plain strings can't express.
concepts.body:
Wherever `find_all` accepts a value (the tag name, an attribute, `string`), you can pass richer **filters**.

A **regular expression** is a pattern for text, written in a small language of its own: `^h[1-6]$` means "h, then one digit from 1 to 6, and nothing else". Python's `re` module handles them, and `re.compile(...)` turns a pattern into an object you can pass around:

- `soup.find_all(re.compile(r"^h[1-6]$"))` matches all headings, h1 to h6.
- `href=re.compile(r"\.pdf$")` matches links ending in `.pdf`.
- The pattern may match anywhere in the value, so start it with `^` and end it with `$` when it must match the whole value.

Other filters:

- A **list**: `soup.find_all(["h1", "h2"])` matches any of them.
- **`True`**: matches anything present: `find_all(True)` is every tag; `attrs={"data-id": True}` is "has data-id".
- A **function**: called with each tag, returning `True` to keep it. For example `lambda t: t.name == "a" and "download" in t.get("class", [])`. When passed for an attribute (`href=func`), it receives the attribute's value (or `None`) instead.

The `string=` argument accepts these too, and then matches pieces of text: `soup.find_all(string=re.compile("total", re.I))` returns the matching **strings**, and `.parent` leads from each back to its tag.

Functions can express any condition, like "a `<td>` with exactly two children" or "an element whose text is a number". Keep them small and give them names, so they stay readable.

CSS selectors can do some of the same with attribute patterns and `:-soup-contains`; choose whichever reads more clearly.
concepts.code:
import re from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """

Report

Q1

Total: 120

Q1 PDF About xy""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") print([h.name for h in soup.find_all(re.compile(r"^h[1-6]$"))]) # ['h1', 'h3'] print([a.string for a in soup.find_all("a", href=re.compile(r"\.pdf$"))]) # ['Q1 PDF'] print(soup.find_all("span", attrs={"data-id": True})) # [x] def is_numeric_total(tag): return tag.name == "p" and re.search(r"\d+$", tag.get_text()) is not None print(soup.find(is_numeric_total).get_text()) # Total: 120 s = soup.find(string=re.compile("total", re.I)) print(repr(s), s.parent.name) # 'Total: 120' p
takeaways: Filters can be strings, regexes, lists, True or functions
A function filter receives each tag and returns True to keep it
string= with a regex returns matching text nodes; use .parent
Regexes are searched, so anchor with ^ and $ when needed
pitfalls: Passing a regex string instead of re.compile(...), which is matched literally.

options: Only tags that are both th and td
All th and all td tags
An error: name must be a string
quiz.explain: A list as a filter matches any of its values.

concepts.name: Scraping real pages with requests
concepts.summary: Download pages with the Requests library, parse them, resolve relative links with urljoin, and scrape politely.
concepts.why: Beautiful Soup only parses, so it's almost always paired with a download library, and that glue code decides whether a scraper is correct and polite.
concepts.body:
Beautiful Soup only parses text you already have. To get a page from the internet, your program does what a browser does when you type an address. It sends a **request** for the page's **URL** (its web address) to the site's **server**, the computer that hosts it, using **HTTP**, the language of the web. The server sends back a **response**: a **status code** saying how it went (200 is OK, 404 is not found) plus the page itself.

The usual Python library for this is **Requests** (`pip install requests`). A minimal scraper:

- Create a `requests.Session()`, which reuses the connection to the site and remembers settings. Set its headers once. **Headers** are labelled notes sent with each request; `User-Agent` names your program, and an honest one includes contact info.
- Always pass a **timeout** (how many seconds to wait before giving up) and call `resp.raise_for_status()`, which raises an exception for error statuses, so error pages never get parsed as data.
- Pass `resp.content` (bytes) to Beautiful Soup and let it find the encoding inside the page itself; `resp.text` relies on what the server claims, which is often wrong.

Links in pages are often **relative** (`/p/2`, `../img.png`): they leave out the site and say where to go from the current page. Combine them with the page's URL using `urllib.parse.urljoin(resp.url, href)`. Use `resp.url`, not the URL you asked for, because the server may have sent you elsewhere (a **redirect**).

Long lists are often split across several pages (**pagination**); scraping them usually means following the "next" link until there isn't one.

Be a good citizen:

- Check the site's terms and its **robots.txt** file, which says what automated programs may fetch (Python's `urllib.robotparser` reads it).
- Pause between requests and don't fire many at once. Sites often enforce a **rate limit** (a cap on requests per minute) anyway.
- Prefer an official **API**: a service that hands out data meant for programs, usually as JSON. Often the page itself loads its data from one; your browser's developer tools (network tab) show it. That's more stable than HTML.
- Save pages to disk while developing instead of downloading them on every run.

If the content isn't in the HTML at all, because JavaScript fills it in later, Beautiful Soup can't see it; see the lesson on robust scrapers.
concepts.code:
import time
from urllib.parse import urljoin
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

session = requests.Session()
session.headers["User-Agent"] = "price-bot/1.0 (+mailto:me@example.com)"

def scrape_titles(start_url, max_pages=3):
    url, titles = start_url, []
    for _ in range(max_pages):
        resp = session.get(url, timeout=10)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        soup = BeautifulSoup(resp.content, "html.parser")
        titles += [a.get_text(strip=True) for a in soup.select("h3 a")]
        nxt = soup.select_one("li.next a")
        if nxt is None:
            break
        url = urljoin(resp.url, nxt["href"])     # resolve relative link
        time.sleep(1)                             # be polite
    return titles

print(scrape_titles("https://books.toscrape.com/")[:2])
# ['A Light in the ...', 'Tipping the Velvet']
takeaways: requests.Session with a User-Agent, a timeout and raise_for_status
Pass resp.content (bytes) so Beautiful Soup detects the encoding
urljoin(resp.url, href) for relative links
Respect robots.txt, pause between requests, and prefer APIs when they exist
pitfalls: Building next-page URLs by gluing strings together, which breaks on relative links.

quiz.q: Why use urljoin(resp.url, href) instead of start_url + href?
options: It resolves relative paths correctly against the final page URL, including after redirects
quiz.explain: urljoin follows the standard rules for combining a page address with a relative link, and resp.url is the address after any redirects.

concepts.name: Extracting tables and lists into data
concepts.summary: Turn HTML tables and repeated blocks into lists of dicts, cleaning text and converting numbers.
concepts.why: Scraped data is only useful once it's organised, typed and ready for a CSV file, a database or pandas.
concepts.body:
Most extraction tasks come down to this: find the element that repeats (a table row, a product card), then build one record, a dict, from each.

For **tables** (`<table>` with rows `<tr>`, header cells `<th>` and data cells `<td>`):

- Read the column names from `thead th` (or the first row), cleaned with `get_text(strip=True)`.
- Loop over the rows in `tbody tr`, skipping rows without `td` cells (section titles, spacers).
- `zip` the column names with the cell texts into a dict.
- Watch for `colspan`/`rowspan`, attributes that make one cell span several columns or rows; they break simple zipping, so handle or reject them on purpose.

For **card lists** (products, articles), select each card and pull out each value with `select_one` inside the card, using a small helper that returns `None` for missing values instead of crashing.

**Clean and convert** right away: strip whitespace, remove currency symbols and thousands separators, turn numbers and dates into real values, and keep the raw text when conversion fails, so you can look into it rather than silently lose data.

For simple, tidy tables, `pandas.read_html()` does all of this in one call (pandas is a popular Python library for tables of data; it uses lxml or Beautiful Soup underneath). Beautiful Soup is the tool when tables are irregular, when you need attributes such as links inside cells, or when the data isn't a table at all.

Finally, check the result: count the records, make sure required values are present, and report anything odd. Silently scraping only part of the data is the classic failure.
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """
CityPop.Link
Paris 2,102,650wiki
Germany
Berlin3,878,100
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") headers = [th.get_text(strip=True) for th in soup.select("#t thead th")] rows = [] for tr in soup.select("#t tbody tr"): cells = tr.find_all("td") if not cells: continue # skip sub-header rows rec = dict(zip(headers, (td.get_text(strip=True) for td in cells))) rec["Pop."] = int(rec["Pop."].replace(",", "")) link = cells[2].find("a") rec["Link"] = link["href"] if link else None rows.append(rec) print(rows) # [{'City': 'Paris', 'Pop.': 2102650, 'Link': '/paris'}, {'City': 'Berlin', 'Pop.': 3878100, 'Link': None}]
takeaways: One record per repeated element (row or card)
Zip column names with cell texts; skip rows without td
Clean and convert types right away
pandas.read_html for simple tables; Beautiful Soup for irregular ones
pitfalls: Zipping headers with cells on tables using colspan, misaligning every column after it.

quiz.q: A table row contains a single <th colspan=3> section title. What should the row loop do?
options: Skip it (or record it as a group label), since it has no td cells
quiz.explain: Sub-header rows aren't records; detect them (no td cells) and skip or use them as context.

concepts.name: Modifying and cleaning HTML
concepts.summary: Change the tree: remove elements with decompose(), edit attributes and text, create tags, and unwrap or replace elements.
concepts.why: Cleaning up content, rewriting links and preparing HTML for emails or text extraction all require editing the tree.
concepts.body:
The tree can be changed, and your changes show up when you turn it back into a string.

**Removing**:

- `tag.decompose()` removes a tag and destroys it with everything inside: use it to strip `<script>`, `<style>`, ads or menus before extracting text.
- `tag.extract()` removes it and **returns** it, so you can insert it elsewhere.
- `tag.clear()` empties the tag but keeps the tag itself.

**Editing**:

- Attributes: `tag["href"] = "..."`, `del tag["style"]`.
- Text: `tag.string = "new text"` replaces everything inside with that text.
- Name: `tag.name = "strong"`.

**Building and moving**:

- `soup.new_tag("a", href="/x")` creates a tag (set `.string` for its text); then `tag.append(child)`, `tag.insert(i, child)`, `insert_before` / `insert_after`.
- `old.replace_with(new)` swaps one element for another.
- `tag.unwrap()` replaces a tag with what's inside it (dropping `<span>` wrappers while keeping the text); `tag.wrap(soup.new_tag("div"))` does the opposite.

Don't change the tree while looping over `.descendants` or anything else that walks the live tree as you go; collect your targets into a list first (`find_all` already returns one).

Beware of using Beautiful Soup to make HTML from strangers safe. Cleaning untrusted input so it can't do harm is called **sanitizing**, and removing `<script>` by hand isn't enough: attributes like `onclick` run JavaScript too, and so do `javascript:` links. For untrusted HTML use a dedicated sanitizer that keeps only an approved list of tags and attributes, such as nh3 or bleach.
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """

Read the docs.

Buy now!
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") for t in soup.find_all(["script", "style"]) + soup.select(".ad"): t.decompose() # drop noise for t in soup.find_all(style=True): del t["style"] # strip inline styles soup.span.unwrap() # keep text, drop wrapper a = soup.a a["href"] = "https://example.com" + a["href"] # absolute link a["rel"] = "nofollow" note = soup.new_tag("em") note.string = " (updated)" soup.p.append(note) print(" ".join(str(soup).split())) #

Read the docs. (updated)
takeaways: decompose() deletes, extract() removes and returns
Edit attributes like a dict; set .string to replace contents
new_tag + append/insert to build; replace_with, unwrap, wrap to restructure
Use a real sanitizer (nh3, bleach) for untrusted HTML
pitfalls: Treating script-tag removal as protection against attackers' JavaScript sneaking into your pages (XSS).
Changing the tree while looping over .descendants, which walks the live tree.

quiz.q: You want to drop <span> wrappers but keep the text inside. Which method?
quiz.explain: unwrap() replaces the tag with its contents; the others remove the text too.

concepts.name: Parsers compared: html.parser, lxml, html5lib
concepts.summary: How the three HTML parsers differ on broken markup, speed and output, and how to parse XML.
concepts.why: Different parsers build different trees from the same broken HTML, which explains scrapers that work on one computer and fail on another.
concepts.body:
Valid HTML parses the same everywhere. **Broken** HTML, which is most of the web, doesn't: each parser repairs it by its own rules. - **html.parser** (comes with Python): decent speed, nothing to install, forgiving but not browser-accurate; doesn't add ``/`` around a fragment. - **lxml**: written in C and the fastest; adds `` around fragments; its repairs can differ from a browser's. - **html5lib**: follows the official HTML5 rules for reading pages, so the tree matches what a browser builds (including ``, and the `` browsers add inside tables); written in pure Python and slow. Example: for `

`, html.parser gives ``, lxml gives ``, and html5lib gives `

`. This matters when you write selectors by looking at the browser's developer tools. The browser added a `` that html.parser and lxml don't add, so `table > tbody > tr` matches nothing. Using html5lib, or selectors that skip `tbody` (`table tr`), fixes it. **XML** needs lxml's XML mode: `BeautifulSoup(data, "xml")` (also spelled `"lxml-xml"`). It keeps upper and lower case in tag names, handles namespaces (prefixes such as `svg:` that keep tag names from different vocabularies apart), and handles self-closing tags like `` properly, which HTML parsers don't. Choose by need: lxml for speed, html5lib for browser accuracy, html.parser for nothing extra to install.
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup broken = "

" for parser in ["html.parser", "lxml", "html5lib"]: try: print(f"{parser:12}", BeautifulSoup(broken, parser)) except Exception as e: # FeatureNotFound if not installed print(f"{parser:12} not installed: {type(e).__name__}") # html.parser # lxml # html5lib

table = "
1
" print(BeautifulSoup(table, "html.parser").select("table > tbody > tr")) # [] print(BeautifulSoup(table, "html.parser").select("table tr")) # [1] xml = '' print([i["id"] for i in BeautifulSoup(xml, "xml").find_all("Item")]) # ['1', '2']
takeaways: Parsers agree on valid HTML and differ on broken HTML
lxml is fastest; html5lib matches browsers; html.parser needs nothing
Browsers add <tbody>; html.parser and lxml don't
Use the 'xml' feature (lxml) for XML documents
pitfalls: Writing selectors with tbody copied from dev tools and getting empty results.

quiz.q: A selector 'table > tbody > tr' copied from Chrome returns [] with html.parser. Likely cause?
options: The browser inserted a tbody that isn't in the raw HTML
quiz.explain: Browsers add implicit tbody elements; html.parser keeps the HTML as written.

concepts.name: Encodings and Unicode, Dammit
concepts.summary: How Beautiful Soup works out a document's text encoding from bytes, how to correct it, and how output encoding works.
concepts.why: Garbled accented characters are the most common silent data-quality bug in scraped text.
concepts.body:
Python strings hold **Unicode**: a catalogue that gives every character of every writing system its own number. Beautiful Soup always works with such strings inside. Give it a `str` and it's used as is. Give it **bytes**, and a component called **Unicode, Dammit** works out which encoding turns those bytes into text.

It tries, roughly in this order: an encoding you pass; a byte-order mark (a few special bytes at the very start that some files use to announce their encoding); the document's own declaration (`<meta charset>`, or the XML declaration); then a statistical guess using chardet, cchardet or charset-normalizer if one is installed; and finally fallbacks like UTF-8 and Windows-1252.

After parsing, `soup.original_encoding` tells you what it decided.

Controls:

- `BeautifulSoup(data, "html.parser", from_encoding="iso-8859-1")` when you know better.
- `exclude_encodings=["windows-1252"]` to rule out a wrong guess.
- `UnicodeDammit(data).unicode_markup` converts bytes without parsing, and `UnicodeDammit.detwingle(data)` fixes documents that mix UTF-8 and Windows-1252.

With Requests, pass `resp.content` (bytes) rather than `resp.text`. Requests decodes `resp.text` using the encoding named in the response's `Content-Type` header, and when an HTML page names none there, it falls back to ISO-8859-1. That garbles UTF-8 pages whose encoding is only declared in a `<meta>` tag.

Garbled text like `CafÃ©` is called **mojibake**: UTF-8 bytes decoded with the wrong encoding.

On output, `str(soup)` and `soup.decode()` give a string; `soup.encode("utf-8")` or `soup.prettify("utf-8")` give bytes, and Beautiful Soup updates the document's `<meta charset>` to match.
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup, UnicodeDammit page = '

Café crème, naïve résumé

'.encode("utf-8") soup = BeautifulSoup(page, "html.parser") # bytes in: detection print(soup.original_encoding, soup.p.string) # utf-8 Café crème, naïve résumé # What resp.text does for text/html without a charset header: wrong = page.decode("iso-8859-1") print(BeautifulSoup(wrong, "html.parser").p.string) # CafÃ© crÃ¨me, naÃ¯ve rÃ©sumÃ© legacy = "Grüße".encode("cp1252") # no declaration at all dammit = UnicodeDammit(legacy, ["cp1252"]) print(dammit.unicode_markup, dammit.original_encoding) # Grüße cp1252 print(soup.p.encode("utf-8")) # b'

Caf\xc3\xa9 cr\xc3\xa8me, na\xc3\xafve r\xc3\xa9sum\xc3\xa9

'
takeaways: Pass bytes so Beautiful Soup can detect the encoding
soup.original_encoding shows the detected encoding
from_encoding / exclude_encodings correct the detection
resp.text can decode a page wrongly; resp.content is safer
pitfalls: Feeding resp.text to the parser and storing mojibake like 'CafÃ©' in the database.

quiz.q: Text shows 'CafÃ©' instead of 'Café'. What usually happened?
options: UTF-8 bytes were decoded as ISO-8859-1/Windows-1252
quiz.explain: Each UTF-8 multibyte character decoded as Latin-1 turns into two odd characters like Ã©.

concepts.name: Robust scrapers and dynamic pages
concepts.summary: Write scrapers that survive layout changes and missing values, spot content added by JavaScript, and know when to switch tools.
concepts.why: Scrapers break constantly; the design choices here decide whether a break is a crash, silent bad data or an easy fix.
concepts.body:
Pages change without notice. A few habits make scrapers resilient:

- **Anchor on meaning, not position**: ids, `data-` attributes, classes that describe content (`price`, `title`), label text ("Price") and structured data, not `div:nth-child(4)`.
- **Use structured data when it's there**: many pages embed **JSON-LD**, a JSON description of the product or article, in `<script type="application/ld+json">`, or **Open Graph** tags (`<meta property="og:...">`) used for link previews. Reading those is far more stable than scraping visible markup.
- **Extract each value in its own small function** that returns `None` when it's missing, then check the records afterwards. If a required value is missing from every record, the layout changed, so stop with a clear error.
- **Save the raw HTML** of fetched pages so you can re-parse after fixing a bug without downloading again.

**Pages filled in by JavaScript**: if data you see in the browser isn't in `resp.content`, JavaScript loaded it after the page arrived. Check "View page source", which shows the HTML as downloaded. The developer tools' inspector shows the page as it is now, after JavaScript changed it (browsers call that live version the **DOM**). Options, from best to worst:

- Find the request that loads the data as JSON in the developer tools' network tab, and call that API directly.
- Read the starting data embedded in a script tag (`window.__INITIAL_STATE__ = {...}`).
- Load the page in a **headless browser** (a real browser controlled by code, such as Playwright), let its JavaScript run, and pass `page.content()` to Beautiful Soup.

For large crawls, with thousands of pages, automatic retries and processing steps for each item, a dedicated scraping framework such as Scrapy fits better than a loop around Requests.
takeaways: Prefer ids, data attributes, labels and structured data over positions
JSON-LD and Open Graph tags are stable data sources
Check records and fail loudly when required values vanish
Content missing from the raw HTML was added by JavaScript: find the API or use a headless browser
pitfalls: Scraping a generated class like pdp-title-x7 that changes every time the site is rebuilt.

quiz.q: Data is visible in the browser's inspector but not in resp.content. Best first step?
options: Look in the network tab for the JSON request that loads it
quiz.explain: The data is fetched by JavaScript; calling that address directly is simpler and more stable than running a browser.

concepts.name: Performance: SoupStrainer, lxml and memory
concepts.summary: Speed up parsing with lxml and SoupStrainer, reduce memory by releasing trees, and know when Beautiful Soup is the slow part.
concepts.why: At thousands of pages, parsing time and memory dominate, and a few switches make a several-fold difference.
concepts.body:
Beautiful Soup is written in Python on top of a parser, and it builds a full object tree with every tag and string. That's convenient but costly. Ways to speed it up:

- **Use lxml** as the parser: typically several times faster than html.parser and far faster than html5lib.
- **Parse only what you need** with a **SoupStrainer**: `BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml", parse_only=SoupStrainer("a"))` builds a tree of just the matching tags and skips everything else. It accepts the same filters as `find_all`. It doesn't work with html5lib, which always builds the whole tree.
- **Pass bytes with a known encoding** (`from_encoding=`) or install a fast encoding detector, since detection can be surprisingly slow.
- **Search narrowly**: find the wrapping element once, then search inside it, instead of running `find_all` over the whole document again and again.

**Memory**: every `NavigableString` you keep holds a link into the tree, which keeps the whole document in memory. Convert results to plain `str` (`str(tag.string)` or `get_text()`) before storing them, and call `soup.decompose()` when you're done with a large document in a program that runs for a long time.

When parsing is still the **bottleneck** (the slowest step, holding everything else up), use lxml's own functions directly (`lxml.html` with XPath, or CSS selectors via cssselect), or a fast HTML5 parser such as selectolax, and keep Beautiful Soup for the messy cases. Measure first with `time.perf_counter()` or a **profiler**, a tool that shows where a program spends its time.
concepts.code:
import time from bs4 import BeautifulSoup, SoupStrainer html = "" + "".join( f'

Item {i}

more
' for i in range(5000) ) + "" def timed(label, fn): t = time.perf_counter(); result = fn() print(f"{label:22} {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s {len(result)} links") timed("html.parser, full", lambda: BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser").find_all("a")) timed("lxml, full", lambda: BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml").find_all("a")) only_links = SoupStrainer("a") timed("lxml + SoupStrainer", lambda: BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml", parse_only=only_links).find_all("a")) # html.parser, full 1.339s 5000 links (timings vary by machine) # lxml, full 0.725s 5000 links # lxml + SoupStrainer 0.582s 5000 links hrefs = [str(a["href"]) for a in BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml", parse_only=only_links).find_all("a")] print(hrefs[:2]) # ['/i/0', '/i/1']: plain strings, tree can be freed
takeaways: lxml is the fastest parser to use under Beautiful Soup
SoupStrainer + parse_only builds only the parts you need
Convert results to plain str so Python can free the tree's memory
For the highest speed, use lxml or selectolax directly
pitfalls: Storing NavigableString objects in a long-lived list, keeping every parsed document in memory.

options: Only matching tags (and their contents) are added to the tree, saving time and memory
It filters results after parsing the full tree
quiz.explain: The strainer is applied while building the tree, so the parts that don't match are never created.

concepts.name: Object model: Tag, NavigableString and more
concepts.summary: Understand the kinds of objects Beautiful Soup creates (Tag, NavigableString, Comment, Script, Doctype) and how they affect text extraction.
concepts.why: Knowing the node types explains why comments or script contents show up (or don't) in your text and how to handle them precisely.
concepts.body:
Every node in the tree is an object of one of a few types, all defined in `bs4.element`. In Python a type of object is called a class, and a class can be a more specific version of another one, called a subclass:

- **`BeautifulSoup`**: the document root, itself a subclass of `Tag`.
- **`Tag`**: an element with `name`, `attrs` and `contents`.
- **`NavigableString`**: text. It is a subclass of `str`, so it works like any string, but it also has tree links (`.parent`, `.next_sibling`), so you can move from a string back to its tag.
- Special kinds of string: **`Comment`** (`<!-- ... -->`), **`CData`**, **`ProcessingInstruction`**, **`Declaration`**, **`Doctype`**, and for HTML, **`Script`**, **`Stylesheet`** and **`TemplateString`** for what's inside `<script>`, `<style>` and `<template>`.

Because they're all strings, a naive `find_all(string=True)` returns comments and script code along with visible text. Check the type with `isinstance(s, Comment)`, or use `get_text()`. By default it includes only ordinary `NavigableString`s and CData, leaving out comments, scripts and styles. That's why `get_text()` on a whole page usually gives readable text without JavaScript.

Attribute values are plain strings, or lists for attributes that can hold several values, like `class`, `rel` and `headers`. Passing `multi_valued_attributes=None` to `BeautifulSoup(...)` turns that off.

`copy.copy(tag)` makes a complete, separate copy you can change without touching the original tree, which is useful for producing cleaned versions.
concepts.code:
import copy from bs4 import BeautifulSoup, Comment from bs4.element import Script, NavigableString html = """

Hello world

""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") for s in soup.find_all(string=True): print(type(s).__name__, repr(s)) # Comment ' tracking id 99 ' # NavigableString 'Hello ' # NavigableString 'world' # NavigableString '\n' # Script 'var x = 1;' print(repr(soup.get_text())) # 'Hello world\n': no comment or script b_text = soup.b.string print(isinstance(b_text, str), b_text.parent.name) # True b clean = copy.copy(soup.div) clean.p.decompose() print(soup.div.p is not None) # True: original untouched
takeaways: Tag, NavigableString and special string subclasses make up the tree
NavigableString is a str that knows its place in the tree
get_text() skips comments, scripts and styles by default
copy.copy(tag) gives a detached copy for safe edits
pitfalls: Collecting find_all(string=True) as 'visible text' and including comments and JavaScript.

quiz.q: Which node type represents <!-- note --> in the tree?
quiz.explain: Comments are kept as Comment objects, which are strings with tree links.

concepts.name: Output: formatters, prettify and entities
concepts.summary: Control how trees are turned back into text: str versus prettify, entity formatters, void elements and indentation.
concepts.why: Producing HTML for emails, page templates or for comparing versions needs faithful, predictable output, not a re-indented approximation.
concepts.body:
There are several ways to turn a tree back into HTML text: - `str(tag)` or `tag.decode()`: compact HTML as parsed (after repairs). Whitespace text nodes are kept. - `tag.prettify()`: one tag per line, indented. Meant for **reading**: it changes whitespace, which can change how a browser displays text inside a paragraph or a `
` block, and it makes before/after comparisons noisy. Don't use it to write documents back.
- `tag.encode("utf-8")`: bytes.

A **formatter** controls how special characters in text and attributes are written, via `formatter=` on `decode`, `prettify` or `encode`:

- `"minimal"` (default): writes only `&`, `<` and `>` as entities, which is enough for valid output.
- `"html"`: writes characters as named HTML entities where possible (`é` becomes `é`).
- `"html5"`: like `"html"`, but writes **void elements** (elements that never have content, like `
`) HTML5-style, `
` instead of `
`, and leaves `&` alone where HTML5 allows it.
- `None`: no escaping at all, which can produce broken or unsafe HTML.
- An `HTMLFormatter` object for full control (indentation, void elements). Note that a bare `HTMLFormatter()` writes no entities unless you pass `entity_substitution`.

Remember that **entities are decoded when parsing**: ` ` becomes the character `\xa0` in the text, and the default formatter writes it back as that raw character, not as ` `. If the output must keep entities, use `formatter="html"`.

Attribute order is kept as parsed. Beautiful Soup puts attribute values in double quotes, switching to single quotes when the value itself contains a double quote.
concepts.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup soup = BeautifulSoup("

Café & bar 
R&D now

", "html.parser") p = soup.p print(repr(p.get_text())) # 'Café & bar\xa0R&D now' print(p.decode()) # minimal:

Café & bar
R&D now

print(p.decode(formatter="html")) #

Café & bar 
R&D now

print(p.decode(formatter="html5")) #

Café & bar 
R&D now

print(p.prettify()) #

# Café & bar #
# R&D # # now # #
takeaways: str()/decode() keep the parsed structure; prettify() is for reading
Default 'minimal' formatter escapes only &, < and >

formatter='html' writes named entities, 'html5' also uses
style
Entities are decoded on parse; choose a formatter to write them back
pitfalls: Saving prettify() output as the cleaned document and changing whitespace-sensitive content.

quiz.q: After parsing ' ', how does str(soup) write it with the default formatter?
options: As the raw non-breaking space character
quiz.explain: Parsing decodes the entity to \xa0, and the minimal formatter doesn't turn it back into an entity.
